parole.significato: The physical blocking or surrounding of a place, especially a port, in order to prevent commerce and traffic in or out.
parole.testo: From block + -ade, probably after Dutch blocquade (now blokkade) or German Blockade.

parole.significato: The effect of a picture appearing within itself recursively, so that the inner picture contains another even smaller pi…
parole.testo: Droste + effect, from Dutch Droste, from German Droste. From the image used on Droste-brand cocoa powder, one of the main Dutch brands, of a nurse carrying a serving tray with a cup of hot chocolate and a box with the same image. parole.significato: An eleven-word poem, successive lines containing one, two, three, four and one words.
parole.testo: From eleven + -ie, calque of Dutch elfje or German Elfchen.

parole.significato: To cut into a surface with an acid or other corrosive substance in order to make a pattern. Best known as a technique f…
parole.testo: From Dutch etsen (“to etch”), from German ätzen (“to etch”), from Old High German azzon (“to cause to bite or feed”), from Proto-Germanic *atjaną, causative of *etaną (“to eat”) (whence also English eat).

parole.significato: An event or a display where fireworks are set off.
parole.testo: From fire + work(s). The similarity with Dutch vuurwerk and German Feuerwerk, both “fireworks”, is hardly coincidental. parole.significato: Synonym of tadpole person.
parole.testo: From head + foot + -er. Possibly a calque of Dutch kopvoeter / koppoter, and/or of German Kopffüßler.

parole.significato: A cannon that combines certain characteristics of field guns and mortars, delivering projectiles with medium velocities…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Dutch houwitser, from German Haubitze, from Middle High German haufniz, from Czech houfnice, which was derived from houf (“flock, crowd”) + -nice. The Czech noun houf comes from Middle High German hufe (“heap”), from Old High German hūfo.

parole.significato: A form of gelatin obtained from the air bladder of the sturgeon and certain other fish, used as an adhesive and as a cl…
parole.testo: Apparently from obsolete Dutch huisenblas, from German Hausenblase, from Hausen (“sturgeon of the Huso genus”) + Blase (“bladder”), with alteration after glass.

parole.significato: A surname from Dutch.
parole.testo: From Diedrich Knickerbocker, the pseudonym adopted by Washington Irving for his 1809 A History of New York, probably for the Knickerbackers of Schaghticoke, New York, descended from the Dutch immigrant Harmen Jansen van Bommel(l), who went variously by the names van Wy(y)e, van Wyekycback(e), Kinnek

parole.significato: A defensive encampment encircled by wagons, especially by South African Boers.
parole.testo: From South African Dutch lager (“camp”) (modern Afrikaans laer), from German Lager, from Middle High German leger, from Old High German legar, from Proto-Germanic *legrą. Doublet of lager and lair.

parole.significato: A hand-operated device with rollers, for wringing laundry.
parole.testo: Ca. 1700, from Dutch mangel, from Early Modern German Mangel (15th c.), enhanced form (by analogy with other tool names in -el) of Middle High German mange, from Medieval Latin manga, manganum, from Ancient Greek μάγγανον (mánganon). Doublet of mangonel.

parole.significato: A piece of work that has been given much critical praise, especially one that is considered the greatest work of a pers…
parole.testo: From master + piece, a calque of Dutch meesterstuk or German Meisterstück (“masterpiece”). Piecewise doublet of maestropiece and masterstick. Compare also journeyman's piece.

parole.significato: A fulmar (Fulmarus glacialis).
parole.testo: Ultimately from Dutch mallemok (from malle (“foolish”)), probably influenced by German Mallemucke. Compare Japanese 信天翁(あほうどり) (ahōdori, “albatross, foolish bird”).

parole.significato: A unit of measurement of land in the Netherlands and the Dutch colonies and parts of the United States, where it was eq…
parole.testo: From Dutch morgen and German Morgen, both literally "morning", probably originally indicated the amount of land that can be ploughed by a team of oxen in a morning. Doublet of morn and morrow.

parole.significato: Dutch, pertaining to the Dutch language
parole.testo: From nether- + Dutch, probably a calque of Dutch Nederduitsch (modern: Nederduits) or a calque of German Niederdeutsch.

parole.significato: Synonym of plagiarist.
parole.testo: From Dutch plagiator and German Plagiator, from Latin plagiātor.

parole.significato: A flat-bottomed boat.
parole.testo: Dutch praam and German Prahm, from Czech prám. Compare Polish prom.

parole.significato: A silver coin and money of account in use from the late-16ᵗʰ to the mid-19ᵗʰ centuries in the European Teutonic countri…
parole.testo: Borrowed from obsolete Dutch rijcksdaler (modern rijksdaalder), after early modern German Reichsthaler.

parole.significato: To scratch (something) with claws or fingernails; to claw.
parole.testo: The verb is a variant of dialectal English scramb (“to pull or rake together with the hands; to gather a handful of something from the ground; to scratch with the claws or nails; to pull down violently; to tear off; to maul about; a handful of something from the ground”), possibly related to Dutch s

parole.significato: To scratch (something) with claws or fingernails; to claw, to scram.
parole.testo: The verb, especially sense 2 (“to scratch with the claws or fingernails”), is possibly related to Dutch schrammen (“to graze, scratch”) and German schrammen (“to scratch, scrape”), from Late Middle High German schramm, schramme (“a graze, scratch”); further etymology unknown. parole.significato: To grind with the teeth, and with a crackling sound; to crunch.
parole.testo: Compare Dutch schransen (“to eat greedily”), German schranzen. Compare crunch, scrunch.

parole.significato: To make a brief, basic drawing.
parole.testo: From Dutch schets or German Skizze, from Italian schizzo, from Latin schedium, from Ancient Greek σχέδιος (skhédios, “made suddenly, off-hand”), from σχεδόν (skhedón, “near, nearby”), from ἔχω (ékhō, “to hold”). Compare scheme.

parole.significato: A whitish, greyish volcanic tufa, formed of decomposed trachytic cinders, sometimes used as a cement.
parole.testo: From Dutch tras or German Trass, probably from Italian terrazzo (“terrace”). See terrace.

parole.significato: Tumultuous, noisy excitement.
parole.testo: Calque of Dutch oproer or German Aufruhr, as up + roar.

parole.significato: Hydrogen.
parole.testo: From water + stuff. Calque of Dutch waterstof (“hydrogen”) or German Wasserstoff (“hydrogen”).
